entries.position: both — a good book, The book is good; in the senses 'large in amount' and 'complete and thorough' only before a noun (a good hour, a good look)
entries.comparison: irregular — better, best
entries.takes: at + noun or -ing for skill (good at chess); with + people or things you handle (good with kids); for + the person or thing it helps (good for your heart); to + a person for kindness (good to me); of + person + to-infinitive (good of you to come); about after feel (feel good about it); to-infinitive (good to know); that-clause (It's good that you called)
entries.contrast: Good is the adjective and well the adverb: She's a good driver / She drives well — She drives good is heard in casual speech but is marked wrong in careful English. After linking verbs use good: It looks good, That smells good. I feel good means happy or in good shape; I feel well means not sick. In American English I'm good means I'm fine and, when you are offered something, No, thanks. Skill is good at (not good in), kindness is good to, benefit is good for: She's good at math, He was good to me, Fish is good for you. The forms are better and best, never gooder or more good. Russian добрый about a person is usually kind, not good.

entries.position: both — a bad idea, The idea is bad

entries.takes: at + noun or -ing for skill (bad at math); with + things you handle (bad with names); for + the person or thing harmed (bad for your back); about after feel for guilt (feel bad about it); for after feel for pity (feel bad for him); to-infinitive (It's bad to skip breakfast); that-clause (It's bad that nobody told her)
entries.contrast: Bad is the adjective and badly the adverb: a bad singer / She sings badly. After linking verbs use bad: It smells bad, I feel bad. I feel bad about it means guilty; I feel bad for him means sorry for him; I feel badly is common in American speech but disliked by careful writers. The forms are worse and worst — more bad is wrong, and badder is only slang. Not bad is praise: it means pretty good. Russian мне плохо is I feel sick or I feel bad, not I'm bad, which means I behave badly. My bad (my mistake) is a slang noun, not this adjective.

entries.comparison: irregular — farther, farthest for distance; further, furthest for distance or degree
entries.contrast: As an adjective far stands before a noun and usually means the more distant of two sides or ends: the far side of the lake. It is not the everyday word for далёкий — say a distant country or a faraway place; a far country sounds literary. It's not far and How far is it? are adverb uses, and plain It's far is informal — It's a long way is safer. The comparison splits: farther and farthest are for physical distance; further and furthest work for distance too and are the only choice for additional (further questions). The far right is a political label (крайне правые), not a direction.

entries.contrast: Little often carries feeling (a cute little house, a nasty little man); small is neutral and is the word to compare: a smaller room, rarely a littler room. For amount, little with an uncountable noun is negative, like мало: We have little time; a little is positive, like немного: We have a little time. Many grammars call this amount use a determiner, and its forms are less and least. With countable nouns use few: few friends, not little friends. In a little tired the word is an adverb, and in I speak a little a pronoun.

entries.position: both — an old house, The house is old; in the senses 'former' and 'known for a long time' only before a noun (my old boss, an old friend)
entries.comparison: -er/-est — older, oldest; elder, eldest only for rank in a family
entries.contrast: Age is be + number + years old, never have: She is ten years old, not She has ten years. Before a noun the phrase is hyphenated and singular: a ten-year-old girl. Position changes the meaning: an old friend is a friend you have known for years, not an elderly one, and my old job is my former job. Older and oldest are the normal forms, in families too (my older brother); elder and eldest go only before a noun and never take than. About people, old can sound blunt — older or elderly is politer.

Later is the comparative (a later flight) and latest the superlative, which also means newest; latter (the second of two) and last (final) have their own entries.

entries.contrast: In everyday American English sick is the usual word and ill is more formal: I'm sick / She is seriously ill. An ill child sounds stiff — say a sick child — but an adverb makes ill normal before a noun (terminally ill patients). In British English sick often means vomiting; in American English it means ill. Before a noun ill usually means bad, not sick: ill effects, ill will. The forms worse and worst belong to both ill and bad: She got worse. Ill- in compounds (ill-advised, ill-treated) is the adverb, and the ills of society is a noun.

Because it only follows a verb, a well man is wrong — say a healthy man. Well the noun (колодец) and the interjection (Well, maybe) are other words.

I'm better means I have recovered; I'm good only means I'm fine. You'd better go (had better) is a modal phrase, and She sings better is the adverb. Better off means in a better situation, richer: We're better off without him. Russian лучший is better when two things are compared (a better car) and the best for all others; careful English says the better of the two.

entries.position: both — the best pizza in town, Which one is best?; before a noun it needs the or a possessive (my best friend)
entries.comparison: irregular — best is the superlative of good and well; the comparative is better
entries.takes: at + noun or -ing (best at math); for + the person or purpose it suits; to-infinitive (It's best to wait)
entries.contrast: Best is already superlative: the best, the very best, never most best. Before a noun it needs the or a possessive — She's the best student, not She's best student. Without the it often means most sensible: It's best to call first. When only two things are compared, careful English uses better: the better of the two, though the best of the two is common in speech. Do your best and at best use the noun, and She sings best is the adverb.

The problem is worse than we thought.

senses.head: Less skillful
examples: I'm even worse at math than my brother.
He's worse with money than anyone I know.

senses.head: More sick; in poorer health
examples: Grandpa got worse overnight.
If your fever gets worse, call the doctor.

entries.position: both — a worse problem, The problem is worse
entries.comparison: irregular — worse is the comparative of bad and ill; the superlative is worst
entries.takes: than + noun or clause; at + noun or -ing (worse at math); for + the person or thing harmed
entries.contrast: Worse is already comparative: much worse, even worse, never more worse or badder. Do not mix it up with worst: This is worse than yesterday (two things) / This is the worst day ever (all others). Worse ends in an s sound, worst in st. Worse off means in a worse situation, poorer. She sings worse than I do is the adverb.

examples: That was the worst meal I've ever had.
He's the worst boss I've ever worked for.
It was the worst decision of her career.
It was the worst storm in fifty years.
The worst part was waiting for the results.
Allergies are worst in the spring.
This is the worst time to buy a house.
You picked the worst possible moment to call.
I was the worst player on the team.
She's the worst at remembering birthdays.

senses.head: Of the lowest quality; worse than all others
examples: That was the worst meal I've ever had.
He's the worst boss I've ever worked for.
It was the worst decision of her career.

senses.head: Most serious, severe or harmful
examples: It was the worst storm in fifty years.
The worst part was waiting for the results.
Allergies are worst in the spring.

senses.head: Least suitable or convenient
examples: This is the worst time to buy a house.
You picked the worst possible moment to call.

senses.head: Least skillful
examples: I was the worst player on the team.
She's the worst at remembering birthdays.

entries.position: both — the worst day, Allergies are worst in spring; before a noun it needs the or a possessive (my worst fear)
entries.comparison: irregular — worst is the superlative of bad and ill; the comparative is worse
entries.contrast: Worst compares something with all others; worse compares two: the worst movie of the year / worse than the book. Never most worst, and baddest is only slang. The worst is over and at worst use the noun. American English says both if worse comes to worst and if worst comes to worst.

examples: The beach was farther than it looked on the map.
Our new office is farther from home, so I leave earlier.
They built a cabin on the farther shore of the lake.
The farther end of the field was flooded.

senses.head: More distant
examples: The beach was farther than it looked on the map.
Our new office is farther from home, so I leave earlier.

senses.head: Being the more distant of two sides or ends
examples: They built a cabin on the farther shore of the lake.
The farther end of the field was flooded.

entries.position: both — the farther shore, The lake was farther than we thought
entries.comparison: irregular — farther is the comparative of far; the superlative is farthest
entries.takes: than + noun or clause; from + a place
entries.contrast: In American English farther is for physical distance and further for distance or degree: The school is farther than the library (further is also fine here) / further questions (only further). Never use farther for additional — farther information is wrong. We walked farther is the adverb. Russian дальнейший is further, not farther.

examples: We sat at the farthest table from the stage.
Neptune is the farthest planet from the sun.
The farthest town on the route is about 200 miles away.
entries.position: both — the farthest point, Which planet is farthest from the sun?
entries.comparison: irregular — farthest is the superlative of far; the comparative is farther
entries.contrast: Farthest is only for physical distance; furthest covers distance and also degree (the furthest thing from my mind). Before a noun it needs the or a possessive: the farthest table. Who can throw the ball farthest? is the adverb.

examples: Call us if you have any further questions.
The office is closed until further notice.
Police are waiting for further information.
The hospital is further than the fire station.
The campsite was further from the lake than the website said.
Nothing could be further from the truth.

senses.head: Additional; more
examples: Call us if you have any further questions.
The office is closed until further notice.
Police are waiting for further information.

senses.head: More distant, in space or in degree
examples: The hospital is further than the fire station.
The campsite was further from the lake than the website said.
Nothing could be further from the truth.

entries.position: both — in the sense 'additional' only before a noun (further details); in the sense 'more distant' also after a verb (The store is further than I thought, Nothing could be further from the truth)
entries.comparison: irregular — further is a comparative of far; the superlative is furthest
entries.takes: than + noun or clause; from + a place or an idea, in the sense 'more distant'
entries.contrast: Further in the sense additional has no farther twin: further information, until further notice, never farther information. For physical distance careful American writing prefers farther, but further is common and correct. Let's discuss it further is the adverb, and to further your career is the verb. Russian дальнейший and дополнительный are both further: further steps, further questions. More further is wrong.

examples: They live in the furthest house on the road.
Which of the moons is furthest from Jupiter?
Retirement is the furthest thing from my mind.
What he told the reporters was the furthest thing from the truth.

senses.head: Most distant
examples: They live in the furthest house on the road.
Which of the moons is furthest from Jupiter?

senses.head: Least likely or least true — in the furthest thing from
examples: Retirement is the furthest thing from my mind.
What he told the reporters was the furthest thing from the truth.

entries.position: both — the furthest house, Which town is furthest?
entries.comparison: irregular — furthest is a superlative of far; the comparative is further
entries.contrast: For physical distance furthest and farthest both work, with farthest preferred in careful American writing. Only furthest is used for degree: the furthest thing from my mind. Before a noun it needs the or a possessive. He went furthest in the tournament is the adverb.

examples: Her elder sister lives in Seattle.
He's the elder of the two brothers.
My elder son is in college now.
The elder Bush was president from 1989 to 1993.
The elder Dumas wrote The Three Musketeers.
At eighty, he is the party's elder statesman.
She has become an elder stateswoman of the tech industry.

senses.head: Older — of one of two members of a family
examples: Her elder sister lives in Seattle.
He's the elder of the two brothers.
My elder son is in college now.

senses.head: Used to tell apart two well-known people with the same name, usually a father and son
examples: The elder Bush was president from 1989 to 1993.
The elder Dumas wrote The Three Musketeers.

senses.head: Senior and respected because of age and experience — mainly in elder statesman
examples: At eighty, he is the party's elder statesman.
She has become an elder stateswoman of the tech industry.

entries.position: attributive only — my elder sister; after a verb only in the elder of the two, never She is elder than me
entries.comparison: irregular — elder is a comparative of old used for rank in a family; the superlative is eldest
entries.contrast: Elder goes only before a noun and never takes than: my elder brother, but My brother is older than me, not elder than me. American English uses older brother far more often; elder sounds formal. It is only for people, mostly in a family: an older car, not an elder car. An elder (a respected old person, a church leader) and respect your elders are noun uses. Elderly means old, not older.

entries.meaning: Oldest — of three or more members of a family. ---
examples: Their eldest daughter just got married.
I'm the eldest of five kids.
As the eldest son, he took over the family farm.
entries.position: attributive only — my eldest daughter; also the eldest standing alone (She's the eldest of four)
entries.comparison: irregular — eldest is a superlative of old used for rank in a family; the comparative is elder
entries.contrast: Eldest is only for people, almost always in a family: my eldest son, but the oldest building, never the eldest building. Oldest works everywhere and is more common in American English. With only two children, elder is traditional (the elder of the two), though eldest is common in speech.

examples: In the latter case, you'll need to apply for a new passport.
Customers can pay online or by phone, and most choose the latter option.
Sales picked up in the latter half of the year.
He spent his latter years in Florida.
The project is in its latter stages.

senses.head: Being the second of two people or things already mentioned
examples: In the latter case, you'll need to apply for a new passport.
Customers can pay online or by phone, and most choose the latter option.

senses.head: Nearer the end of a period of time
examples: Sales picked up in the latter half of the year.
He spent his latter years in Florida.
The project is in its latter stages.

entries.position: attributive only — after the, this or a possessive (the latter option); the latter also stands alone for the second of two
entries.comparison: not gradable — once a comparative of late, now fixed in meaning
entries.contrast: Latter (rhymes with matter) and later (rhymes with waiter) are different words: the latter half is the second half; a later date is a date further in the future. Use the former and the latter only for two things; for three or more say the last. It is formal and mostly written — in speech Americans usually say the second one. The latter often stands alone: Of the two plans, the latter is cheaper.

examples: Don't skip the last chapter.
She was the last person to leave the office.
The last train leaves at midnight.
We went to Boston last weekend.
Last night's game went into overtime.
I saw him last Tuesday.
The last time I saw her, she was still in high school.
Prices have doubled over the last few years.
His last email was pretty rude.
Can I have the last cookie?
I spent my last ten dollars on gas.
He's the last person I expected to see here.
A flat tire is the last thing I need right now.

senses.head: Coming after all others; final
examples: Don't skip the last chapter.
She was the last person to leave the office.
The last train leaves at midnight.

senses.head: Just before this one — with week, month, year, night and days of the week, without the
examples: We went to Boston last weekend.
Last night's game went into overtime.
I saw him last Tuesday.

senses.head: Most recent
examples: The last time I saw her, she was still in high school.
Prices have doubled over the last few years.
His last email was pretty rude.

senses.head: Only remaining
examples: Can I have the last cookie?
I spent my last ten dollars on gas.

senses.head: Least likely or least wanted
body: (последний (о ком или чём меньше всего ожидаешь))
examples: He's the last person I expected to see here.
A flat tire is the last thing I need right now.

entries.position: both — mostly before a noun (the last page); after a verb in be last (She was last in line)
entries.comparison: not gradable — once a superlative of late; the very last adds emphasis
entries.contrast: Last week, last year and last Friday take no article and mean the one before this one: I saw her last week. The last week means the past seven days, or the final week of something: The last week has been crazy / the last week of June. Last means final or the one before now, while latest means newest: his last book may be his final one, his latest book is his newest, with more to come. For news and updates say the latest, not the last. At last is an adverb phrase, He finished last uses the adverb, and to last is the verb.

examples: Have you seen her latest movie?
Download the latest version of the app.
The latest polls show a close race.
What's the latest time we can check out?
The latest flight to Miami leaves at 10:40.
Friday is the latest date we can accept your application.

senses.head: Newest; most recent
examples: Have you seen her latest movie?
Download the latest version of the app.
The latest polls show a close race.

senses.head: Happening after all others in time
examples: What's the latest time we can check out?
The latest flight to Miami leaves at 10:40.
Friday is the latest date we can accept your application.

entries.position: attributive only — after the or a possessive (the latest news); the latest standing alone (Have you heard the latest?) is a noun use
entries.comparison: -er/-est — latest is the superlative of late; the comparative is later
entries.contrast: Latest means newest, most recent, and more may follow: her latest album. Last means final, or the one before now: her last album may be her final one. For news, trends and versions English says latest, not last: the latest news, the latest update. At the latest means no later than: by Friday at the latest. Late in the sense dead has no latest.

examples: We'll cover that in the next chapter.
The next day, it snowed.
Who's next in line?
My parents are visiting next month.
Next summer we're going to Maine.
I have a dentist appointment next Thursday.
The music from the next room kept me awake.
She lives in the next town over.
The couple at the next table were arguing.

senses.head: Coming right after this one in time or order
examples: We'll cover that in the next chapter.
The next day, it snowed.
Who's next in line?

senses.head: Just after this one — with week, month, year and days of the week, without the
examples: My parents are visiting next month.
Next summer we're going to Maine.
I have a dentist appointment next Thursday.

senses.head: Nearest in place; right beside
examples: The music from the next room kept me awake.
She lives in the next town over.
The couple at the next table were arguing.

entries.position: both — mostly before a noun (the next day); after a verb in be next (You're next)
entries.comparison: not gradable — once the superlative of nigh, an old word for near
entries.contrast: Next week, next year and next Monday take no article and mean the one after this one: See you next week. With the, next counts from some other time: We arrived on Monday and left the next day. Next Friday can be unclear in American speech — some people mean the coming Friday, others the Friday after — so this Friday is safer for the coming one. Next is about order and nearest about distance: the next gas station is the next one on your route, the nearest gas station the closest in any direction. Next to (рядом с) is a preposition, and What happened next? is the adverb.

examples: Where's the nearest gas station?
The nearest hospital is forty miles away.
Take the seat nearest to the door.
This is the nearest thing to real Mexican food in town.
His nearest relative is a cousin in Ohio.
Round the answer to the nearest whole number.
Prices are rounded to the nearest dollar.

senses.head: Closest in distance
examples: Where's the nearest gas station?
The nearest hospital is forty miles away.
Take the seat nearest to the door.

senses.head: Closest in relationship or likeness
examples: This is the nearest thing to real Mexican food in town.
His nearest relative is a cousin in Ohio.

senses.head: Rounded to a given unit — in to the nearest
examples: Round the answer to the nearest whole number.
Prices are rounded to the nearest dollar.

entries.position: both — the nearest hospital, Which exit is nearest?
entries.comparison: -er/-est — nearest is the superlative of near; the comparative is nearer
entries.takes: to + noun (the seat nearest to the door)
entries.contrast: Nearest is about distance, next about order: the nearest exit is the closest one, the next exit is the one you reach after this one on the highway. Unlike plain near, nearest stands freely before a noun: the nearest store, never a near store. In everyday American speech closest is more common. To the nearest dollar means rounded (с точностью до доллара).
